platforms.title: Eczema vs. Contact Dermatitis: It's Not the Same Rash
platforms.meta_description: Red, itchy skin and no idea why? How the AAD tells eczema apart from contact dermatitis — by location, onset, and its link to a specific substance.
platforms.body_html:
Red, itchy skin, and no matter what you try it just won't clear up? The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) explains that eczema and contact dermatitis come from completely different causes. Without telling them apart, switching from one product to another can mean staying exposed to whatever's actually causing it while it never really heals.

Why a similar-looking rash has different causes

Eczema, also called atopic dermatitis, is a chronic condition tied to the skin's barrier function and immune response. It commonly shows up in the creases of the elbows, behind the knees, and on the neck, usually starts in childhood, and tends to recur over many years. A family history of hay fever, asthma, or allergies is common alongside it.

Contact dermatitis comes from an entirely different cause. It's marked by a reaction to a specific substance that touched the skin directly, with the rash forming exactly where that substance made contact. New cosmetics, nickel in jewelry, or the spot where a ring or watch sits often line up precisely with where the rash appears.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether the rash lines up exactly with where a specific substance touches the skin. The AAD notes this is the clearest sign of contact dermatitis. Eczema shows up repeatedly in the same set locations, like the inner elbows or behind the knees, regardless of any particular substance.

Second, whether it's been there since childhood, or lines up with a recently started product. Eczema usually goes back to childhood, while contact dermatitis tends to overlap with when a new product or piece of jewelry was first used.

Certain jobs and habits raise the odds of contact dermatitis, including hairdressing, cleaning, healthcare work, and any job involving frequent handwashing, latex gloves, or exposure to solvents and fragrances. Common triggers include nickel in jewelry and belt buckles, fragrances in lotions, preservatives in cosmetics, and rubber accelerators in gloves. Eczema flares are triggered differently, often by dry cold air, sweating, wool clothing, or stress, rather than any single product. Because both conditions can overlap in someone with a naturally sensitive skin barrier, a dermatologist visit is worth it whenever a rash lingers beyond a couple of weeks despite basic care.

What matters most is not trying different products one after another while still exposed to whatever's actually causing contact dermatitis. Without removing the trigger substance, even the best product won't stop it from coming back. Eczema management centers on steady moisturizing to repair the skin barrier, while contact dermatitis calls for identifying and avoiding the exact trigger first.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether the rash's location lines up exactly with a specific substance, when it first started, whether there's a family history, and whether any new cosmetics or jewelry have been introduced recently. If the trigger is hard to pin down, a dermatologist can confirm it with a patch test.

Is your rash in a familiar spot you've had since childhood, or does it line up exactly with something you've recently started wearing or using?
